1:
Chrysostom notices first that the apostle is adjusting his argument to the age of his hearers. Paul builds his discourse as a man forms a body, head then neck then feet — husband, then wife, then children — and when he reaches the children he says nothing of Christ and nothing on high subjects, because he addresses tender understandings; he keeps it short, since children cannot follow a long argument; and he sets aside the kingdom for what a child's soul most longs to hear, that it shall live long. Calvin asks a related question about the choice of words: why command obedience when honour has the wider meaning? Because obedience is the evidence of what is owed, and the harder part, for the human mind recoils from subjection —, and he asks whether one child in a thousand is found obedient. Gill takes honour to cover thought, word and gesture, and adds the maintenance of aged parents, which the Jews explained as giving them food, drink and clothing and leading them in and out. Wesley notes that the mother is named particularly, as being more liable to be slighted than the father. He draws the terms as widely as they will go, taking in illegitimate and adopted children and children-in-law, and among parents the step-parent, the guardian, the nurse and every ancestor.

What obedience in the Lord qualifies is disputed. Henry sets out three construals and prefers the least obvious: some take it as a limitation, as far as is consistent with duty to God; he takes it rather as a reason, obey them for the Lord's sake; or else as a specification of the matters in which obedience is chiefly due. Calvin holds parents are to be obeyed only so far as is consistent with piety to God, which comes first in order. Clarke gives both senses, adds that the clause is wanting in several reputable manuscripts and in some versions, and concludes that no child is called to obey a parent who commands what is unreasonable or unscriptural. Cyril guards the point from the other side: when fathers on earth are of a contrary mind to our Father in heaven we must obey Christ's word, but he insists that the Lord did not say whoever loves father or mother is unworthy of him — he added the words more than me, lest anyone should perversely mistake what was rightly written.

The claim that this is the first commandment with promise raises an old difficulty, and the answers converge. Barnes, Calvin and Wesley all answer alike: the mercy promised in the second commandment is a general declaration attaching to the whole law, not a promise annexed to that precept, so the fifth alone carries one of its own. Robertson reaches it by grammar, reporting that some take first to mean first in the order children are taught and judging that the added words point the other way; he notes too that the word for long-lived occurs nowhere else in the New Testament.

What the promise covers then divides them. Ellicott observes that by dropping the words which the Lord thy God giveth thee, Paul generalises the promise and fixes it on the earth rather than on the good land of heaven, as the meek inherit the earth and godliness has promise of the life that now is. Calvin argues identically and independently, that Moses named Canaan because the Jews could conceive no happier life, and that Paul left the place out because its distinction lasted only till the coming of Christ. Barnes defends the desire for long life as a longer space to prepare for eternity. Wesley alone pulls the other way, allowing that it is usually fulfilled to dutiful children but holding that under the Christian dispensation the promise is to be understood chiefly in a more exalted and spiritual sense.
4:
Gill catalogues the ways a father provokes his children, by words and by deeds: unreasonable commands, reproachful language, public chidings; then preferring one child to another, withholding necessaries or recreation, cruel blows, denying them education, disposing of them badly in marriage, and spending the estate so as to leave them nothing. Clarke draws a distinction of motive instead — parents are called to correct their children, not to punish them, since punishment proceeds from revenge and correction from affectionate concern; he adds that cruel parents generally have bad children, and that a father correcting according to God and reason feels every blow on his own heart more than the child feels it on his body. Barnes makes it reciprocity: if obedience is required, the commands must be such as can be obeyed. Calvin warns that harshness makes children throw off the yoke, and that the word for bringing up conveys gentleness — then notices Paul checking his own concession, drawing the rein again where he had slackened it, against the opposite evil of indulgence. Gill and Wesley agree on why fathers rather than mothers are addressed: fathers are apt to be too severe, as mothers are too indulgent.

On the two words for education Ellicott and Robertson disagree. Ellicott takes nurture for training by discipline and admonition for putting in mind by word, and holds that both carry a tinge of severity befitting ancient education, the first being the same as the chastening of Hebrews. He adds that Christianity gradually softened the stern paternal authority of Roman law by the addition of the words of the Lord, the children belonging not to the parent only but to Christ. Robertson resists the narrowing, reporting that the papyri support the wider sense of a child's general education and culture, and that only some argue for chastening here.

The passage on servants forces each commentator to say what he thinks of slavery, and they disagree. Clarke is the most violent: in heathen countries slavery was in some sort excusable, but among Christians it is an enormity and a crime for which perdition has scarcely an adequate punishment — and in the same breath he holds that a Christian slave was bound to serve faithfully the man whose money bought him, however illegal that traffic be reckoned. Barnes argues that the word need not mean a slave at all, and that Christianity was designed to modify the customs of society gradually rather than sunder them; yet at the next verse he turns the text into an indictment, observing that a hired freeman may be trusted out of sight where a slave may not, that this is why drivers are necessary, and that the evil is unavoidable except where religion prevails — whose prevalence would set the slave free. Henry expects the same outcome sooner, that teaching both parties their duty would lessen the evils until slavery should be rooted out, masters and servants being fellow-servants in respect of Christ. Ellicott finds the limitation already in the phrase according to the flesh: slavery can subjugate and even kill the body but cannot touch the spirit, and the slave is a man in immortal being and not the living tool that philosophy called him. Chrysostom is blunter — slavery is nothing but a name, the mastership according to the flesh and therefore brief. Calvin describes the institution exactly — perpetual unless the master granted freedom, bought with money for degrading work, the power of life and death protected by law — and warns servants not to imagine the gospel had procured them carnal freedom. Gill explains why Paul enlarges here: less pains were taken to instruct servants, and false teachers were insinuating that servitude was inconsistent with Christian liberty. Robertson notes that Paul rejoiced to call himself a slave of Christ, and that God's will may be done even by the slaves of men.
7:
Barnes uses this passage to forestall the use that would be made of it. He grants that the servant should serve faithfully until he may enjoy liberty peaceably; then he turns to the master and forbids two inferences — that because a pious slave shows this spirit he therefore thinks his master right to withhold his freedom, and that because religion commands submission it therefore approves what the master does. It approves it, he says, no more than it sanctioned Nero or Mary by requiring the martyrs to submit to them. At the next verse he states it flatly: religion does not approve of slavery, it is the friend of human rights, and with full influence on earth it would restore every man to freedom; Christianity nowhere requires anyone to make or own a slave, and no one under its proper influence ever yet made a man one.

Ellicott reaches the same end by a different route, through the slave who is called in the Lord and becomes the Lord's freeman: that conception, logically worked out, has ultimately destroyed slavery, and meanwhile it gave the slave in his slavery — lightened though not yet removed — the power of serving with good will. On the recompense he presses the wording, which says not that a man receives the reward of his deed but that he receives the deed itself, still living and returning on his head; and he notes what makes that promise necessary, that a slave in law had no rights and therefore neither responsibility nor hope.

Calvin is the most exact about what he is describing. The command to serve with good will is set against the suppressed indignation that swells in the breast of slaves, who dare not openly break out but obey with the greatest reluctance; and he remarks that anyone who reads the ancient accounts of the dispositions of slaves will see that the number of injunctions here does not exceed the number of the diseases needing cure. He applies it to his own century: servants now being in a far more agreeable condition, they are the less excusable if they fail. He also refuses the world's valuation: it sets little value on a slave's labour, but God esteems it as highly as the duties of kings, judging each by the uprightness of his heart.

On the masters, the argument turns on where their limit comes from. Calvin observes that the laws granted masters vast power, that whatever the civil code sanctioned was widely taken to be lawful in itself, and that the cruelty went so far the emperors were forced to restrain it; yet God allows a master no power beyond what the law of love permits. He then finds the philosophers short: they urge that slaves be treated like hired servants, but never look beyond utility, and even there ask only what suits the head of the family, whereas the apostle asks what masters owe. Ellicott reads the ban on threatening the same way, since threatening implies coercion from a position of tyrannical superiority, treating a man as one who must be driven like a brute-beast rather than led; and he explains that respect of persons means regard for the mask of outward condition. Clarke would have punishment lean toward mercy and be as light as possible, revenge excluded as of the devil, and quotes the rabbinic saying that a rich man will hear a rich man and ignore a poor one, but that before God women, slaves, the poor and the rich are all alike. Gill sets out what a religious master owes — instruction, prayer, good example, time for religious duties, food and raiment or due wages, and care in sickness. Wesley asks that masters act from the same principle, and Robertson observes that Paul, addressing the lords of the slaves, is afraid neither of capital nor of labour.
10:
The opening address produces an immediate clash. Ellicott judges the words my brethren an interpolation, probably drawn in from Philippians, since the compellation appears in neither this epistle nor the Colossian. Wesley builds on the very word Ellicott would delete, noting that it occurs only here in the epistle and that soldiers frequently use it to each other in the field. Henry supplies the frame: our life is a warfare and our religion much more so, and we have enemies to fight, a captain to fight for, a banner to fight under and rules of war to keep. A soldier must be stout-hearted as well as armed — strong for service, for suffering, for fighting — since however well armed without, a man with no good heart within will find his armour stand him in little stead. Calvin raises the objection against himself: what purpose is served by enjoining a strength they cannot supply? His answer is that the sentence has two clauses, one exhorting to courage, the other directing them to ask God for what they lack. Wesley presses the strange phrasing, as if God's might would not do and it must be the exertion of his might; Robertson observes that it is not a hendiadys.

On the armour they divide between the antiquarian and the moral. Robertson identifies the panoply from Polybius as shield, sword, lance, helmet, greaves and breastplate, notices that Paul omits the lance and adds the girdle and shoes, not armour but necessary to a soldier, and remarks that Paul could fairly claim to know a Roman soldier's equipment, having been chained to one for some three years. Clarke adds that the word denotes the armour of the heavy troops who sustained the rudest attacks and stormed cities, and glosses the wiles as the methods of the devil — a man's method of sinning being Satan's method of ruining his soul. Barnes takes the point twofold: the weapons are God's providing, not such as men employ, and must be worn entire rather than in part. Ellicott agrees the emphasis falls on completeness, leaving no point unguarded by a carelessness that may prove fatal at all, and identifies putting on this armour with putting on Christ. Calvin puts the charge as a picture: a soldier who takes his helmet and neglects his shield, or leaves his arms hanging on the wall. Cyril reads it through the rite of anointing — forehead, ears, nostrils and breast — so that those who have put on the breastplate of righteousness stand against the devil as Christ went out after his baptism and vanquished the adversary.

Who the adversaries are is the last question. Clarke alone reports a human answer, that Schoettgen took the rulers of this darkness for the rabbins and Jewish authorities; the rest take them for spirits. Wesley maps them, guessing that the principalities remain mostly in the citadel of their kingdom while other spirits range abroad with the provinces committed to them. Clarke renders spiritual wickedness as the spiritualities of wickedness — refined and sublimed evil, falsehood disguised in the garb of truth. Ellicott prefers the order blood and flesh and suggests the word blood stands first to prevent any momentary confusion with wrestling against the flesh as an evil power within us; and adds that a struggle with wicked men may admit some reserve of sympathy, while this is a truceless war. Calvin makes the comparison exact — sword against sword, man against man, force met by force and skill by skill — and draws the lesson that we should remember it when ill treatment provokes us to revenge. Robertson collects the word for world-ruler from the Orphic hymns, from Gnostic writings, from the rabbis where it names the angel of death, and from imperial inscriptions; Gill reports that several versions read you where ours reads we.
13:
A single participle divides them. Clarke insists the clause means having conquered all, stand — a military phrase used so by the best Greek writers, and produces a sentence from Dionysius of Halicarnassus to prove it. Barnes agrees that the word means to vanquish, so that safety comes only when the last enemy has fallen; Robertson puts it as standing when the wrestle is over, as victor. Ellicott stands alone against them and against Chrysostom, whom he names: the rendering having overcome all is tempting but does not accord with Paul's use of the word, and the sense is rather that when we have done all we are called to do, we plant our feet firmly, the one word conveying activity and the other a calm steadfastness. On the evil day itself Wesley observes that the war is perpetual though the fight is more violent on one day than another, while Ellicott holds that in this life all days may be evil but, except to the reprobate, none wholly so. Clarke adds that the ancient heroes were fabled to have armour sent them by the gods, and that Paul speaks not of fable but of reality.

Chrysostom explains the order of the argument. Arms would have been useless had the soldiers not first been posted in rank and their spirit roused, for a man must be armed within before he is armed without — and in the spiritual case, he adds, there is no arming without at all. He notes too that the first thing in tactics is to know how to stand well.

How far the pieces should be interpreted is itself contested. Calvin refuses the exercise: an allusion to military custom is all that was intended, and nothing can be more idle than the pains some have taken to discover why truth is made a girdle rather than a breastplate. Barnes says much the same, doubting whether the reason can be determined at all. Ellicott instead traces both pieces to Isaiah, where righteousness is the girdle of his loins and a breastplate besides, and observes that another epistle assigns the breastplate to faith and love. On the breastplate a confessional inversion appears. Calvin rejects the reading that makes it a freely bestowed or imputed righteousness, holding such matters out of place here because the subject under discussion is a blameless life; Wesley takes it as precisely the righteousness of spotless purity in which Christ will present us faultless through the merit of his own blood. Wesley also notices what is not in the list: the breast is the seat of conscience, and no armour for the back is mentioned, because we are always to face our enemies.

The shoes raise the hardest question, and the answers cross the usual lines. Ellicott works through three possibilities and rejects two: the natural appeal to the beautiful feet of them that preach is inappropriate here, because every other piece of the armour is a quality and not a function; readiness will not do either, since readiness of the gospel is hardly intelligible; so he settles on the derived Septuagint sense of a foundation or base. Gill reaches the identical conclusion by the same route, that the word signifies a base as the Septuagint uses it, giving the soldier firm footing in a solid knowledge of the gospel. Clarke takes the rejected first option, citing the passover eaten with the feet shod, and holds that a readiness to publish the gospel is meant; Barnes reports the same from his lexicon. Calvin takes the middle course, that the gospel equips us for journey and battle alike, since by nature we dislike exertion and are discouraged by the smallest annoyance. Robertson glosses it briefly as the readiness of mind the gospel gives, and Wesley as what enables us to tread the rough ways and hold out to the end.
16:
Barnes settles the first phrase against the obvious reading: above all does not mean most important but over all, as a soldier holds a shield that can be turned in any direction and so covers the other pieces. He and Robertson and Clarke then describe the object — the large oblong shield rather than the small round one, of light wood or a brass rim faced with hides and kept anointed so arrows glance off, its name taken from the word for a door. Clarke identifies the fiery darts with the missile called the falarica, headed with lead; Robertson compares the burning arrows shot to set fire to an enemy's camp. Ellicott asks instead which faith is meant, and rules two out: not the faith in which we stand, nor the energetic faith of the eleventh of Hebrews, but a patient trust on which the darts of fear or lust or doubt fall harmless — adding that the best commentary on the words is Christian's conflict with Apollyon in the Pilgrim's Progress. Cyril supplies such a case: faith shut the lions' mouths for Daniel, and quenches a dart of base desire by suggesting a picture of the judgment. Calvin first denies the distinctions can be pressed — faith and the word are one thing, the word being faith's object and faith nothing without it, and elsewhere the apostle gives faith a breastplate instead — then allows that the two most necessary weapons rightly answer to faith and to the word.

The helmet produces a genuine division. Barnes, Wesley and Calvin all import the parallel passage where it is the hope of salvation, Barnes observing that a soldier will not fight well without hope of victory, Calvin that the head is protected when hope lifts us toward what is promised, and Wesley grading the hope from confidence that God will finish his work in us up to full assurance of glory. Ellicott alone resists. The word here is not the usual term for salvation but a general expression for what tends to it, drawn from Isaiah; the metaphor is therefore different, and the helmet is salvation in the concrete, received in earnest now and hoped for in perfection later. He notes too that the verb changes from putting on to receiving. Clarke offers a different explanation altogether, that Greek helmets bore emblematic figures on the crest and that Paul may refer to one displaying hope. On the sword they agree: it is the single offensive weapon, and Wesley marks the turn — until now the armour has been defensive, but we are to attack as well as secure ourselves, the shield in one hand and the sword in the other.

Prayer is then added, and Clarke argues from the structure that it is not part of the armour at all: had it been, the apostle would have matched it to some Grecian piece as he did the other six, so the catalogue is finished and prayer is what equips the man who wears it — though Greek armies did sacrifice before engaging. Calvin asks why continuance is enjoined twice over and answers that the repetition is not idle: when everything goes prosperously we feel no strong excitement to prayer, and never flee to God except when driven by distress, so the command covers prosperity as well as adversity. Wesley turns on a particular party, those who use only mental prayer and ejaculations and think their worship far superior, when it requires much more grace to pour out a fervent and continued prayer than to offer mental aspirations. Gill calls prayer the last weapon and requires it in times of darkness and desertion especially; Barnes remarks that soldiers do not often feel the necessity of it; and Robertson answers with a couplet, that Satan trembles when he sees the weakest saint upon his knees.
19:
That Paul asks for prayer at all is the first thing noticed. Calvin infers that no man is so richly endowed as to need no such help while he remains in this world, and asks who could plead exemption better than Paul; Gill agrees that the superior members need the assistance of the inferior. Calvin then raises the harder question — does Paul betray unbelief by doubting his own steadfastness and begging the intercession of others? — and answers that he seeks no remedy outside the divine promise. He also disposes of the suggestion that the apostle was held back by fear: the danger was rather that a splendid beginning might not be sustained. Henry adds the detail that makes the request strange, that Paul had so great a command of language they called him Mercury, because he was the chief speaker.

What he asks for divides them. Clarke reports that the phrase for giving utterance is shown by many examples to mean permission and power to defend oneself in court, which fits an ambassador in bonds expecting a public hearing — and holds that Paul got what he asked, since his imprisonment turned out to the furtherance of the gospel. Calvin rejects that reading in advance: Paul asks not for the powers of an acute debater, or rather of a dexterous sophist, to shield himself from his enemies by false pretences, but for a clear and strong confession, since a half-shut mouth utters only confused sounds. Ellicott corrects the translation — the words mean that word may be given him in the opening of his mouth, the opening being assumed — so what is sought is the promise that it shall be given in that hour what to speak. Robertson says Paul wants their prayer for courage; Henry finds three requests — freedom from restraint, ability to express himself, and boldness to deliver the whole counsel of God.

The ambassador in chains draws the strongest writing in the chapter. Barnes observes that an ambassador is a sacred character and no greater affront can be offered a nation than to imprison one; Wesley makes the contrast in a line, that the ambassadors of men appear in great pomp, and how differently the ambassador of Christ appears. Ellicott supplies the physical fact: the word means a single chain, distinguished from the fetter that binds the feet, so a manacle binding the hand, pointing to the custom of chaining a prisoner by the wrist to his guard — Paul being free except for that one chain, which the soldier was responsible for holding and perhaps did not always think it needful to hold. He adds that Paul speaks of the chain as the badge of his ambassadorial dignity: it belongs to ambassadors to be safe from imprisonment, but it was his greater glory to wear it. Robertson notes that the word for ambassador comes from the word for an old man, and that Paul, now old, felt the dignity of the office even in a chain. Barnes will not stop at Paul: we should pray for the prisoner, the captive, the man in chains and the slave, and he counts them — some ten thousand prisoners in his own country, children of crime but also children of sorrow, and near three millions of slaves, sunk in ignorance and want and woe.

On Tychicus they assemble a biography from scattered notices, from Asia and the journey to Jerusalem to the carrying of this letter and the Colossian one, with the Greeks making him one of the seventy and a bishop. Calvin explains why he was sent — uncertain or false reports produce uneasiness even in steady minds — and admires that a man with death before his eyes provided for the most distant churches where another would have said his own affairs required all his attention.
22:
The close of the epistle raises a question about the epistle itself, and two commentators of different schools arrive at the same doubt by different roads. Clarke reports the dispute openly: whether the letter went to the Ephesians or the Laodiceans is contested, Lardner arguing strongly for the first and Paley for the second. Then he states the objection he cannot meet — if it was really sent to Ephesus, a church the apostle knew so intimately, it is strange he names no person in it; and this objection, on which Paley lays great stress, he says has not been successfully answered. Ellicott, without mentioning the controversy, finds the same difficulty in the benediction: it is impossible not to notice the difference between the generality here, the brethren and all who love the Lord Jesus Christ, and the personal you of every other epistle — a difference he calls inexplicable if the letter were addressed to Ephesus alone. He also observes that the salutation of grace is what Paul himself calls the token in every epistle, written with his own hand, absent from the letters of James, Peter, Jude and John and present in Hebrews, and that here uniquely it is made conditional.

What that love must be to qualify divides them over a single word. Ellicott insists the original is far stronger than sincerity: it means incorruptibility, a word ordinarily used of the immortality of heaven and applied to human character only here and in one other place, so that the love meant is immortal and imperishable. Robertson agrees in three words, calling it a never diminishing love. The others take it of the lover rather than of the love. Calvin, following Erasmus, holds that Paul states indirectly that a heart free from hypocrisy will be free from corruption, and turns it against his own generation: most men will make some professions of religion while entertaining exceedingly low notions of Christ and worshipping him with pretended homage, and he wishes there were fewer instances in his own day to prove the admonition still necessary. Clarke says the same of his — many profess to love the Lord who are corrupt in all their ways — and requires love to be proved by holiness of life. Wesley takes it both ways, of not corrupting the genuine gospel and of having no mixture of corrupt affections, and adds continuance until grace issues in glory.

On the peace of the preceding verse Calvin weighs whether the word carries the force of a salutation or means concord among themselves, and decides the second agrees better with the context, since the prayer teaches that love and faith no less than peace are gifts bestowed through Christ. Ellicott traces the order instead — peace first with God in the thankful receiving of his mercy, then love with faith toward him, and out of that peace and love toward men. Gill takes the peace to include prosperity outward and inward and especially peace of conscience under the sprinkling of Christ's blood; Barnes notes the form was the common Eastern greeting and remains so.

The two closing notes are about the manuscript. Clarke observes that the final Amen is missing from several of the best copies, though likelier genuine here than most such subscriptions, and that the word implies not a wish that it may be so but the faithfulness of him who gave the promises. Barnes judges that the subscription to this epistle, like the others, carries no authority, but that in this instance there is every reason to think it correct — and then breaks off to address his reader directly, that nothing will be more needful at the close of life than the consciousness of loving Christ sincerely, and that the evidence of it will then be better than all the wealth toil can gain or the honours the world can bestow.
